sections.html: Hobbs lies in eastern Lea County less than 4 miles from the Texas border and anchors the Hobbs micropolitan area. It grew from 34,122 people in 2010 to 40,508 in 2020, seventh among New Mexico cities. Lovington holds the county seat, yet Hobbs sees the bulk of local housing sales. US 62/180 runs through town, with Seminole, Texas, 29 miles east and Carlsbad 69 miles west.

sections.h2: Oil cycles and what they mean for owners
sections.html:
Hobbs began as a homestead in 1907 and became an oil town after the Midwest Oil Company struck oil in 1927. A refinery opened the next year, and the town incorporated in 1929. More than 12,000 people lived here at the first boom's peak. The Depression cut that to about 3,000 by 1931, and drilling brought it back to roughly 14,000 by 1940.

That swing has not gone away. Lea and Eddy counties together accounted for nearly 1.0 million barrels a day, or 52 percent, of U.S. crude oil production growth between 2020 and 2024. The biggest local industry is oil and gas extraction, then retail trade and educational services. If you bought close to a peak and now face a quieter year, a local agent or buyer can describe how oilfield work is moving demand on your side of town.

Not all work depends on drilling, which gives the market some stability beyond the oil cycle. Schools, colleges and retail add steady jobs, and the Urenco enrichment plant in nearby Eunice draws technical workers to the area.

The city calls flooding one of the biggest hazards in the greater Hobbs area, and it can happen with little or no notice. Severe weather, extreme heat and drought, grass fires and power outages are also listed. Land drains east toward Seminole Draw or southeast toward Monument Draw, so water follows the low points.

Since 1992 Hobbs has belonged to the National Flood Insurance Program and its Community Rating System. Its Class 8 rating trims flood insurance premiums by 10 percent for residents. Where a flood zone only touches a property line, coverage may cost less and is not required. Elevation certificates are on file with the city, handy for a buyer whose house is in a Special Flood Hazard Area; the Engineering Department answers at (575) 397-9232. Summer highs average in the mid 90s, and thunderstorms, hail, lightning, tornadoes and wind-driven grass fires all occur on the high plains.

Gather these before listing:

  • The address's FEMA flood zone
  • An elevation certificate, if the city has one
  • Roof age and hail or wind repair records
  • Past flood or storm insurance claims

Permits for building, electrical, mechanical and plumbing jobs come from Building Safety and Permitting, inside the Planning and Engineering Department. It is at 200 E. Broadway Street, phone (575) 391-8158. Permits cover new buildings, additions, remodels, demolitions, manufactured homes, re-roofs, HVAC, fireplaces, pools, decks, fences and curb cuts, and the office posts re-roofing guidelines and a homeowner permit application. The current residential code is the 2021 New Mexico Residential Building Code, effective January 1, 2024.

Think back over every project since you bought. Did each have a permit? An inspector may check. For a re-roof, deck or bathroom remodel done without paperwork, ask the office how to close the file, or say so to a cash buyer at the start so the price accounts for it. Code Enforcement is at (575) 391-4178. Property outside the city limits needs a Lea County address and a new construction application first, so confirm your property is inside Hobbs before calling.

Two installments cover the year. November 10 is the first deadline, with delinquency after December 10, and April 10 is the second, with delinquency after May 10. The Lea County Treasurer collects on behalf of the county, cities, school districts, the State of New Mexico and other taxing bodies, and mails bills built on the County Assessor's valuation.

Tax gets settled at the closing table. The title company requests the balance from the Treasurer, subtracts it from your proceeds and splits the current year between you and the buyer. An inherited house with several unpaid years needs a heads-up to the title company early, since delinquent taxes can end in a state tax sale once the statutory period runs out.

Putting the house on the market makes sense if it is in good condition and you have time for showings and repair requests. When time or condition is the obstacle, selling for cash fits better. A job change, a rented house, an inherited property still in a relative's name, or storm damage insurance only partly covered can all point toward a direct sale.

  • Request each buyer's written offer along with a proposed closing date.
  • Find out who covers title, escrow and recording costs.
  • Make sure funds move through the title company.
  • Do not sign anything that gives a buyer an open-ended option without payment.

No price is guaranteed. An offer reflects the house, its location and the repairs it needs.

sections.h2: What buyers ask before they commit
sections.html:
Expect questions about three things. First, water: does the lot drain well, and is any part in a flood zone? Second, the roof and exterior after hail or wind. Third, paperwork: permits, tax status and any insurance claims. A short written answer to each puts you in a stronger spot and shortens negotiations.

If you are unsure on any point, call the right office instead of guessing. The city handles flood and permit questions, and the county Treasurer handles tax balances. Writing down the date and the answer you received gives the title company something firm to work with.

sections.h2: Selling a rental or inherited house
sections.html: Two owner types come up often. A landlord may want to hand the house over with the tenant in place, or empty. An heir may live elsewhere and hold a house still titled in a relative's name. In both cases, tell any buyer the facts early: who occupies the house, who can sign, and what taxes are open. A cash buyer can plan around a tenant or probate timeline when told up front, and a surprise discovered late is what ends deals.

sections.h2: Getting ready to sell step by step
sections.html: Walk the property the way a buyer will. Begin on the roof, because hail and wind produce the most repair requests on the high plains. Check the HVAC next, since summers run hot. Then put permit records, the newest tax bill and any insurance claim papers in one folder. A cash buyer who takes the house as it is will not ask you to fix any of it, but the folder helps the title company and keeps the closing on schedule.

faqs.q: Is Hobbs in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Some areas do, and the city warns that flooding can strike with little notice. Look up your address on the FEMA map or call Hobbs Engineering at (575) 397-9232.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a building permit in Hobbs?
faqs.a: Call Building Safety and Permitting at (575) 391-8158, at 200 E. Broadway Street. Code Enforcement is at (575) 391-4178.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Lea County?
faqs.a: November 10 and April 10 are the two due dates, with delinquency following on December 10 and May 10. Ask the Lea County Treasurer to confirm amounts before you pay or close.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Hobbs house with a hail-damaged roof?
faqs.a: Yes. Cash buyers generally accept the roof as damaged and lower the offer to match, while a mortgage buyer may require repairs first.

faqs.q: Do I need to fix unpermitted work before selling in Hobbs?
faqs.a: Not always, though inspectors may ask to see permits. Ask the city how to close one out, or sell to a cash buyer who accepts the house unchanged.
